claims.text: Integrating ab initio molecular dynamics with machine-learning-enhanced CALPHAD can predict melting and liquid-phase properties across a broad compositional range of high-entropy alloys.
The target high-entropy alloys contain multiple principal elements with complex interactions.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can generate the raw thermodynamic data needed by the integrated framework.
Machine-learning algorithms can calibrate and refine CALPHAD models for high-entropy alloys.
Entropic stabilization and phase equilibria play a prominent role in high-entropy alloys with moderate numbers of principal elements.
Short- and medium-range ordering forms and evolves in the solid phase and transitions into the liquid phase.
The evolution of short- and medium-range order mediates melting and fusion-related properties.
Ab initio simulations capture electron–ion interactions that determine fusion properties.
Ab initio simulations capture vibrational contributions that determine fusion properties.
Machine learning can identify complex correlations in multicomponent systems and use them to adjust CALPHAD parameters.
Machine-learning adjustment of CALPHAD parameters refines predictions of phase-transformation thermodynamics.
The improved CALPHAD model provides faster and accurate predictions of key liquid-phase properties.
The integrated approach will predict melting temperatures to within approximately ±50 K of experiment.
The integrated approach will predict enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting to within approximately ±5% of experiment.
The integrated approach will significantly outperform conventional experimental and standard CALPHAD methods.
Traditional experimental methods may require extensive experimental calibration.
Standard CALPHAD approaches without machine-learning integration often have larger prediction errors for high-entropy alloys.
The approach is mainly applicable to well-controlled high-entropy alloys containing moderate numbers of constituent elements.
Extreme compositional disorder may reduce the predictive performance of the approach.
Melting regimes dominated by kinetic effects, such as rapid solidification, may reduce the predictive performance of the equilibrium approach.
